g.text: We found 1 sign of malicious activity. This is not an ordinary outage: restarting the router will not
The device with MAC 08:00:27:3a:66:9e keeps claiming to be 192.168.1.15, 192.168.1.1 (162 ARP claims, 149
On a local network, devices use ARP to ask 'who has this IP address?' and trust whoever
answers. Here a device keeps sending fake answers saying that 192.168.1.1 lives at its MAC address
08:00:27:3a:66:9e. Devices that believe it send their traffic to the impostor, which can read or modify it
before passing it on, so the network may only feel slow or flaky to users. Because the impersonated
address is your router, internet traffic can pass through the attacker.
Like someone changing the house numbers on your street so your post is delivered to them first.
ARP cache poisoning from the device with MAC 08:00:27:3a:66:9e (its own address is
192.168.1.66), for example a tool like arpspoof, ettercap or bettercap.
1. Find the device: look up MAC 08:00:27:3a:66:9e in your switch's MAC address table (or the router's
client list) to get its port or Wi-Fi name, then disconnect it.
2. Check your own ARP cache with
3. As a temporary measure, pin the router:
4. Enable Dynamic ARP Inspection (with DHCP snooping) and port security on managed switches.
5. Treat passwords typed while this was happening as exposed: change them, and prefer HTTPS/VPN.
Why we think it's an attack
The suspicious MAC answered ARP for 2 different IPs that belong to other devices (192.168.1.15,
The disputed address 192.168.1.1 belongs to the router (default gateway)
The suspicious MAC 08:00:27:3a:66:9e sent 149 ARP replies nobody asked for
Not two devices are using the same ip address: Some signs pointed this way (Both MACs answered the same
ARP question 6 times, which is what two honest devices with the same address do), but they were
outweighed. The stronger evidence: The suspicious MAC answered ARP for 2 different IPs that belong to
